title: AI is Not the Solution to All Our Educational Challenges
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Nick Potkalitsky, an AI-in-education writer, argues after a week-long experiential trip with 25 ninth graders that AI will not solve the most pressing problems in education. He lists the accumulated crises of American schooling since 2000, notes that ChatGPT arrived as a hoped-for solution and became another problem, and then offers ten observations about post-pandemic students for which AI is no remedy. These include fragile emotional resilience, weak concentration, difficulty with multi-step tasks without scaffolding, dependence on handheld technology, hunger for connection, a craving for outdoor space and movement, and a need for multiple pathways and ownership of their learning. He adds that students distrust school as normal and watch how adults respond to AI with surveillance and bans. He concludes by proposing an immersive mindset as the foundation for AI-responsive instruction.
points: Potkalitsky's core claim is that social-emotional dynamics, not technology, drive and inhibit academic goals in post-pandemic students.
Concrete classroom adjustments are suggested: repeated attention cues, scaffolded multi-step tasks, brain breaks, and postponing summative grading until mastery.
Students' hunger for connection and their pull toward immersive flows is tied to handheld dependence and the loneliness that followed the pandemic.
Natural settings recentre students, leading him to argue for purposeful engagement with nature beyond recreation.
Surveilling and banning moves by schools are read by students as signals of distrust, so rebuilding trust requires clear expectations and real ownership.
quotes: While I am very excited about the future of AI in schools, I must admit after a week on an experiential learning trip with a group of 25 9th graders that AI will not likely solve the most pressing educational problems in the first half of the 21st century.

The issue then became: How do we get AI to do the work of solving these other controversies and problems? And yet, after only a few days in circulation, the solution itself became another problem as students around the world rushed to use the software to generate unique, “undetectable” responses to assignments and essay prompts. But this dynamic is no surprise to veteran educators.

Students continue to have significant difficulties concentrating and engaging with routine tasks in classroom and real world settings in the wake of the global pandemic. When asked to focus during a quick check-in or conversation, students need as many as 3 to 4 reminders before the majority of the group is ready to engage with a particular thought, direction, or objective. Use of hand gestures, verbal call-and-response, invitations to students to rephrase directions, etc. greatly assist in helping students attend to small details.
Regardless of one’s response, the core problem seems clear. Today’s students hunger for connection. The loneliness pandemic is still in full effect.

Students continue to face significant challenges occupying and inhabiting space inside traditional school buildings. However, when situated in more natural settings like playgrounds, parks, hiking paths, or forests, they become more centered, attentive, focused, and joyful.

Small gestures are big gestures to this current generation. This generation knows that it needs guidance, but desires the kind of assistance that empowers. The question is: Are we ready to offer such assistance?

Our students need the room to relearn how to be responsible for themselves. It is time to scale back the restrictive measures. It is time to make our expectations clear, but also give students space in applying them to their lives.
